data: f, err := syntax.ParseAll(src) lines := syntax.Deparse(f.Exprs[0], nil) // deparse(), one string per line syntax.Deparse is in v0.2.0 and completes milestone M1 (parser and deparse).
data.known-divergences#Known divergences:
Both are platform effects, not semantics.
exp10. Numeric constants with a decimal exponent beyond about 200 in magnitude: R takes a power of ten from the C library’s exp10, which on macOS is not always the correctly rounded value. 5 of 100 000 random literals of that kind (1e229, 1e303, 1e-244) deparse with one more digit in Go (1.00000000000000e+229). No such constant occurs in R’s sources or tests. x86-64 long double. On x86-64 Linux, where R parses and formats numbers in 80-bit long double with its own digits routine, 6 of the 90 files of R’s tests/ deparse with a different last digit in some constant (1e-270 against 9.99999999999999e-271, -5152.07935578853 against ...52). The CI lane on Linux reports that verdict and gates the other three columns and all of src/library.
data.parity-with-r-462#Parity with R 4.6.2:
Judged by the oracle: the same input is parsed, then deparsed by R and by Go, for deparse() and print().
Corpus Inputs Deparse R src/library: every .R file of the base packages (7.8 MB) 844 (842 parse, 2 rejected) 842 / 842 R tests/: 95 files (1 is not UTF-8 and is skipped) 94 (90 parse, 4 rejected) 90 / 90 our snippets 42 42 / 42 our deparse cases (parentheses, precedence, line breaking, indentation, constants, names) 65 (2 rejected) 63 / 63 differential fuzz: 610 000 random edits of lines of R’s sources 610 000 all decimal literals, random (up to 20 digits, exponents -330..330) 100 000 99 995 identical, 5 not The complete table, with the tree, token and error columns, is on The parser.
data.what-it-is-written-from#What it is writt: Deparse is written from the documented behaviour of deparse(): precedence and parenthesisation, the 60-byte line cutoff with its break points and indentation, if/else layout inside braces, structure-free constants, 15-significant-digit numbers, and string escapes with R’s own table of printable characters. That table is generated by the oracle into syntax/print_gen.go, and the list of primitives that deparse as function calls into syntax/prims_gen.go. No R source is copied.

The package is github.com/go-embedded-r/r/eval, in v0.10.0 (bounded by default since v0.4.0).
s := eval.NewSession(eval.Options{}) // bounded by default since v0.4.0 res, err := s.Eval("f <- function(x, y = 2) x * y; f(21)") // one notebook cell res, err = s.EvalContext(ctx, src) // the same, cancellable res.Value, res.Visible // the last value, whether R would print it res.Output, res.Stderr // what print/cat and the auto-print wrote; message() output res.Warnings // []eval.Warning{Message, Call} // err is *eval.Error{Message, Call, Condition, Output, Stderr, Warnings} (R's own text), // *syntax.Error or *syntax.LimitError; a timeout or a cancel unwraps to context.DeadlineExceeded / Canceled s.Get("x"); s.Set("x", v) // the global environment persists from one cell to the next
data.evaluating#Evaluating: Eval(src) parses the source and evaluates its expressions in order in the global environment, as one notebook cell. The result is that of the last one. EvalContext(ctx, src) is the same, and ends with an *eval.Error wrapping the context’s error when ctx is done. EvalIn(ctx, src, env) is EvalContext in the given environment, a child of the global one for a cell that must not leave names behind. Get(name) and Set(name, v) read and write the global environment.
data.limits-bounded-by-default#Limits: bounde:
Since v0.4.0 the zero eval.Options{} is bounded. This is a breaking change: before it, MaxSteps, MaxAlloc and Timeout were unbounded unless set. A zero field now selects its default:
Option Meaning Default MaxSteps calls and loop iterations evaluated by one Eval 30 000 000 MaxAlloc bytes of vector storage allocated in total by one Eval, copies included 16 GiB Timeout time one Eval may take; a context given to EvalContext bounds it too 10 s MaxDepth nesting of evaluations (R’s expressions); beyond it, evaluation nested too deeply 5000 MaxVector length of any vector the runtime allocates 2^28 elements Parse a syntax.Limits bounding the source text of an Eval see syntax.Limits The first three defaults were measured, not guessed (RGO_MEASURE=1 go test -run TestMeasureLimits -v ./eval): the 1 035 goldens of v0.5.0 need at most 8 879 steps, 0.8 MB and 3 ms, and the heaviest cells a notebook runs on purpose (a loop of 10^6 iterations: 3 million steps, 0.17 s; a list grown by 20 000 assignments: 1.6 GB of copies, 0.63 s) set the scale. Each default is about ten times that.
A limit that is hit ends the evaluation with an R error that names it and leaves the session usable.
Opting out is explicit. To remove a limit, say so: MaxSteps: eval.Unbounded (also for MaxAlloc and Timeout; eval.Unbounded is -1). A zero never means unbounded, and any other negative value panics in NewSession. Use Unbounded only for trusted code. A context given to EvalContext still stops an unbounded session.
The bomb tests (while (TRUE) 0, numeric(1e12), 1:1e12, unbounded recursion, an allocation loop) assert a refusal under a Go memory limit, and in CI under ulimit -v.
data.maxalloc-is-a-budget-not-live-memory#Max: MaxAlloc counts every byte of vector storage one Eval allocates, copies included, over the whole evaluation. It is a cumulative budget, not the memory alive at any moment: a cell can stay far below 16 GiB resident and still spend it. The 16 GiB default is sized for a native process. An embedder with little memory, such as a WebAssembly one, should set MaxAlloc much lower.
data.result-and-errors#Result and errors:
Result carries Value, Visible, Output (what print() and cat() wrote, and the auto-printed value of every visible top-level expression, as an R console shows them), Stderr (message() output) and Warnings (the warnings raised and not muffled, each with its message and call).
An error is an *eval.Error with Message (R’s conditionMessage), Call (the deparsed conditionCall, empty for none), Condition (the condition object that was signalled; nil for limits and interrupts), and the Output, Stderr and Warnings the cell had produced before it failed. Its text is R’s: Error in f(1) : object 'y' not found. A parse failure is a *syntax.Error or a *syntax.LimitError.
data.session#Session:
NewSession(Options) makes one interpreter: a global environment that persists from one Eval to the next, so names assigned by one cell are seen by the next.
A Session is not safe for concurrent use. Cells run one at a time; an embedder that serves several callers uses one session per caller, or serialises the calls itself.

Status: M2 is complete (slices 1 to 4), in v0.7.0 (pull request 12, 2026-11-07): 175 of R’s 210 primitives and 110 base closures, 1 154 of 1 154 goldens at that release. The other 35 primitives are refused with an error that says why (eval.Unsupported, listed by go run ./cmd/rparity missing, not counted as implemented): the complex and raw types, S4, formulas and expression vectors, foreign calls (.C, .Call, .External*, .Fortran, lazyLoadDBfetch), .Internal, and the tracing and debugging primitives. M3, base R, has started: see M3 plan / base coverage.
Later releases, all 2026-11-07: v0.7.1 (pull request 13) takes tre v0.1.1 and streams the sub/gsub loop (BenchmarkGsubGroup, 20 000 lines: 247k to 87k allocations per operation, 9.0 to 4.6 MB per operation; the timing against R is deferred because of machine load, so no speed is claimed). v0.8.0 (slice 5) starts the base library: our own R in eval/baselib/*.R (BSD, clean room) plus Go natives, 1 202 of 1 202 goldens, vector fuzz 18 000 of 18 000, base coverage 22.2 %. v0.8.1 (pull request 16) takes tre v0.1.3. v0.8.2 (pull request 18) makes arithmetic, comparison and &/| on two arrays with different dims raise R’s non-conformable arrays, and an array against a longer vector raise dims [product n] do not match the length of object [m] (zero-length arrays are fine, as in R); it also keeps dimnames padding in step (both were FuzzEval crashers). v0.9.0 and v0.9.1 (slice 6) add the string and format functions. v0.10.0 (slice 7) adds restarts and the call stack, 1 302 of 1 302 goldens, base coverage 24.4 % (23.3 % at v0.9.0). Slices 6 and 7 are described below.
History: slice 2 was released in v0.3.0 (pull request 8); v0.4.0 (pull request 9) bounded the session limits by default; v0.5.0 (pull request 10, 2026-11-05) added slice 3; v0.6.0 (pull request 11, 2026-11-06) made its regular expressions a port of TRE (v0.5.0’s were an approximation on Go’s regexp); see Regular expressions. The design is docs/m2-design.md; the API is on Eval API.
data.coverage-102-of-rs-210-primitives-and-94:
Slice 1: constants and symbols, environments, <-/=/<<-, function and closures with R’s three-pass argument matching, promises (lazy arguments, missing, ...), {, if, for, while, repeat, break, next, return, quote, and arithmetic, comparison and logic with R’s recycling, NA rules, type promotion and integer overflow; c, list, length, is.*, as.*, sum/prod/min/max/any/all, abs/sqrt/floor/ceiling/exp, seq_len, seq_along.
Slice 2:
replacement functions with copy-on-modify (x[i] <- v, x[[i]] <- v, x$a <- v, names(x) <- v, attr(x, "a") <- v, f(g(x)) <- v, user "f<-" functions); [, [[ and $ with R’s drop, NA, out-of-bounds, negative, partial-matching and matrix/array rules; attributes (attr, attributes, class, dim, dimnames, levels, structure; factors keep levels); S3 (UseMethod, NextMethod, internal dispatch on [, [[, $, their assignment forms, length, print, and the group generics Ops, Math, Summary); the condition system (stop, warning, message, signalCondition, tryCatch with finally, withCallingHandlers, try, on.exit, the restarts muffleWarning and muffleMessage, suppressWarnings, suppressMessages, custom conditions); print and auto-print that reproduce R’s text for atomic vectors, named vectors, lists, matrices and arrays, factors, conditions, closures and attributes (R’s formatReal with 7 digits, [k] labels at width 80). Slice 3:
environments as values (environment, environment<-, new.env, globalenv, emptyenv, baseenv, parent.env, parent.frame, sys.call, sys.function, assign, get, get0, exists, mget, ls, rm, local, eval, evalq, list2env, as.environment); the apply family (lapply, sapply, vapply, Map, mapply, Reduce, Filter, Find, Position, do.call, match.fun); character functions (nchar, substr, substring, strsplit, sprintf, format, toupper, tolower, casefold, chartr, trimws, startsWith, endsWith, Encoding, enc2utf8, utf8ToInt, intToUtf8, validUTF8); regular expressions (grepl, grep, sub, gsub, regexpr, gregexpr, regmatches): POSIX extended syntax with leftmost-longest matching, on a Go port of TRE since v0.6.0 (see Regular expressions). Slice 4 (v0.7.0) completes M2: the rest of the math group (log family, trigonometric and hyperbolic functions, gamma family, trunc, sign, round and signif with R 4’s rounding algorithm), cumsum/cumprod/cummax/cummin, range, is.finite/is.infinite/is.nan, anyNA, nzchar, switch, substitute, nargs, ...length/...elt/...names, call, as.call, forceAndCall, ::/::: (resolved in the base and global environments), %*%/crossprod/tcrossprod, seq.int, proc.time, and typeof, mode, deparse, as.name, unique, duplicated, match, %in%, factor, levels, format of factors. Collation is decided and documented: see M3 plan / base coverage.
Slice 7 (M3, v0.10.0) adds restarts (withRestarts with functions and arguments, computeRestarts, findRestart, invokeRestart(r, ...), tryInvokeRestart), the call stack (sys.nframe, sys.calls, sys.frames, sys.frame, sys.on.exit), Recall, match.call (positional, partial and exact matching, ... expanded from the caller, expand.dots), errorCondition, warningCondition, geterrmessage, and $ on a call. A calling handler or finally no longer changes the visibility of the value.
Slice 6 (M3, v0.9.0 and v0.9.1) adds string functions: strrep, substr<-, strtoi, make.unique, basename, dirname, formatC (formats d, f, e, g, s; flags -, 0, +, space; big.mark; negative width), prettyNum, toString, sQuote/dQuote (curly quotes, as the oracle’s UTF-8 locale gives), shQuote, noquote and print(quote = FALSE), file.path; part 2 adds format(big.mark =), formatC(mode =, format = "fg"), shQuote(type = "csh"/"cmd"/"cmd2") and match.arg, and sprintf("%#x", 0) prints no prefix, as C does. Text produced by sprintf, formatC and strrep counts against MaxAlloc.
Slice 5 (M3, v0.8.0) starts the base library. eval/baselib/*.R is base R’s glue written by us, BSD, under the clean-room rule of the M3 plan (isTRUE, isFALSE, xor, Negate, setNames, union, intersect, setdiff, is.element, append, head, tail, ifelse, nrow, ncol, NROW, NCOL, lengths, rep_len, diff, outer), embedded, parsed once and evaluated into the base environment of each session (43 µs per NewSession). Go natives: as.vector, order, rank (average, first, min, max), pmax, pmin, which.max, which.min, tabulate, rowSums/colSums/rowMeans/colMeans, t, diag, mean, stopifnot.
matrix, array, letters and LETTERS are there for the tests. Each primitive and each of the 110 closures (print, cat, paste, tryCatch, structure, inherits, …) is exercised by the goldens; the rest of the 35 primitives that remain are refused with an error that says why. Errors and warnings are R’s own: Error in f(1) : object 'y' not found.
data.design-choices#Design choices: Clean room. R’s C code is a specification, never a source. The design is written from the R Language Definition, R Internals, the help pages and what the oracle (GNU R 4.6.2) does; each slice is checked by the oracle lane before it is merged. Bounded. Recursion depth (R’s own expressions limit, 5000), vector allocation size and evaluation steps are session limits, refused with R’s own error, never a Go crash. Typed Go slices for vectors, not []interface{}: arithmetic loops run over []float64 and []int32, and NA is a value inside the slice (R’s INT_MIN and NaN-payload conventions), never a side bitmap. Calls are *Lang with an argument slice, not pairlists; a real pairlist type is only for formals, attributes and pairlist(). Attributes are an ordered slice, because their order is observable. Symbols are interned, so quote(x) == quote(x) is pointer equality. *Missing is its own type, for f(x, ) and missing(). No byte-code: the AST walker is the semantics; a faster tier would be a later, measured decision. Closures take promises: lazy arguments, missing, ..., with R’s three-pass argument matching (exact name, unique partial name, position). Lexical control flow is not panic-based on the hot path (break, next, return travel as a flow code); errors and non-lexical exits use a typed Go panic recovered at the owning context. Conditions: handlers are a stack on the session. Exiting handlers unwind with a typed panic caught by their tryCatch, calling handlers run with the stack truncated below them, and restarts are found by name. Errors are signalled as conditions before they end the evaluation, so tryCatch(error=) and withCallingHandlers(error=) see them. Replacement functions use always-copy semantics; the ownership optimisation stays deferred. The oracle judges. Goldens are R’s answers to inputs written in the repository, compared byte for byte; the tests replay them without R.

Comparison classes, counted: exact for everything except 5 644 libm cases (trigonometric, hyperbolic, logarithmic, gamma, expm1, log1p, log(x, base)) compared within 4 ulp, where the largest difference seen is 2 ulp (log, log10) and 1 ulp for the others; and 335 gamma-family cases (lgamma, digamma, trigamma) compared through signif(x, 12) because our routines are less accurate than R’s (open issue 14). sinpi, cospi, tanpi agree exactly 20 000 / 20 000 FuzzEval: random source never panics, hangs or allocates without bound (the corpus keeps the 13 crashers it found) about 70 million executions in the last runs, clean
data.known-divergences#Known divergences:
Of slice 2:
[[<- with a vector subscript on a list that goes through an NA, an absent name or a logical (x[[c(1, NA)]] <- v, x[[c("a", "c")]] <- v on an unnamed list): R’s message comes from its recursive indexing and ours differs (31 of 26 000 fuzz cases in the earlier run). A few R messages for [[<- on atomic vectors with 0, negative or NA subscripts follow the oracle for the common cases only. Function printing: print of a function does not show R’s address (a placeholder), and .Primitive formals are not shown. Printing an array with more than 2^20 slices or 2^22 rows is refused instead of running for ever. print of list elements dispatches only to the methods R registers itself (factor, condition), as R does. Of slice 7 (v0.10.0), all because R runs tryCatch and try through closures we do not have:
the conditionCall of a stop() made directly inside try() or tryCatch() at top level is empty here, and R’s internal call there (doTryCatch(...), try(...)); match.call(expand.dots = FALSE) keeps ... as a list where R keeps a pairlist (deparse shows list( for pairlist(); absolute frame numbers differ from the oracle’s, which runs each snippet inside its own harness frames, so the goldens compare numbers of frames relative to a starting point; computeRestarts has no top-level abort restart. Of slice 5 (v0.8.0):
A matrix whose dimnames carry names (names(dimnames(x)), as table() makes) prints without the variable-name header lines R adds. lgamma, digamma and trigamma are less accurate than R’s: an open defect, issue 14; the fuzz compares them through signif(x, 12) and counts them. mean sums in float64 (with R’s second pass) where R uses long double: last-bit differences are possible on long sums. The math fuzz compares libm functions within 4 ulp (largest seen: 2), not exactly: the last bit of those functions depends on the C library. Of slice 3:
Regular expressions: TRE’s approximate-matching syntax is not ported, non-ASCII classes use Go’s Unicode tables, perl = TRUE is refused, and grepl is 1.44 times slower than R (an open defect); see Regular expressions. sort of non-atomic values is not implemented. Collation (decided in slice 4): strings sort and compare as R 4.6.2 does under the oracle’s C.UTF-8, which is ICU order, not code point (punctuation, digits, letters; accents after the plain letter; lowercase before uppercase). Strings outside Latin script compare by code point after the Latin letters, a documented divergence. See M3 plan / base coverage. Widths of sprintf and format above 2^24 are refused. sprintf("%05d", NA) zero-pads the NA as macOS does, where glibc pads with spaces (the C library decides in R, so the golden leaves it out). From the platform rather than the semantics:
The bits of a NaN (its sign, whether it is quiet) are whatever the hardware made of it, so goldens and the fuzz compare NA against NaN, not their payloads. exp and the power with a fractional or negative exponent can differ from the C library’s pow/exp in the last bit (the fuzz keeps the exponents integral and leaves exp out; they come with go-numerics in M4). The 2 of 190 000 arithmetic fuzz cases are one of each (a pow last bit, and NA %% 3 added to a NaN). min/max of a character vector mixed with numbers is not collated like R’s. The modulus family is written with explicit fused multiply-adds, as R is compiled on arm64, so it gives the same result everywhere; R on x86-64 Linux does not fuse, so its %% of huge doubles can differ there (the CI lane reports the evaluator fuzz on Linux, it does not gate it).
data.not-started#Not started: M3 (base R) is in progress. M4 to M8 (stats, graphics, notebook bridge, wasm playground, CRAN ports) are planned.

go-embedded-r/r is BSD-3-Clause (see its LICENSE). The sources of R are GPL-2-or-later, so:
R is an oracle, never a source. R is run as a black box and what it prints is recorded. No R source file, no R test file, no R help page, no .Rout.save transcript and no text of R’s manuals is copied into the repository, and none is downloaded at run time. The golden files are the answers of R 4.6.2 to inputs written there. Base R’s R code is rewritten, not copied. The R-language parts of the base packages (base, stats, utils, methods, …) will be re-implemented under the BSD licence from the documented behaviour and from what the oracle does. Fetching the GPL code on first use, and a GPL port, were considered and rejected (decision of 2026-11-01, recorded in the roadmap). Contributors work from specifications: the R Language Definition, the R Internals manual, the help pages, and the oracle’s behaviour. Do not open src/main, src/nmath or the R code of the base packages while writing the counterpart. See CONTRIBUTING.md and NOTICE.

M3 has started. M2 gave an evaluator with 175 of R’s 210 primitives; M3 is the rest of what library(base) exports (1 152 closures). The first slice of M3 is in v0.7.0 (pull request 12); slice 5, which starts the base library, is v0.8.0, slice 6 (strings and format) is v0.9.0 and v0.9.1, slice 7 (conditions and the call stack) is v0.10.0, the current release. The plan is docs/m3-plan.md.
data.collation-decided-in-slice-4#Collation (: R 4.6.2 started with LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 (the oracle’s locale) still orders strings with ICU, not by code point: sort(c("b", "A", "a", "B")) is "a" "A" "b" "B", punctuation sorts before digits before letters, and accents come after the plain letter. The evaluator reproduces this for Latin text (eval/collate.go: three-level comparison, ICU’s order of the ASCII punctuation), for sort, order, ls, < and > on strings, and min/max of strings; == is exact. Strings outside Latin script compare by code point after the Latin letters (a documented divergence). method = "radix" and LC_COLLATE=C will select code-point order when Sys.setlocale exists (slice 6).
data.gates-per-slice#Gates, per slice: goldens from our own snippets, compared with the oracle byte for byte (value, visibility, output, stderr, warnings, error message and call); a differential fuzz mode for the new area, with every exclusion counted; FuzzEval for the whole evaluator, each crasher kept in the corpus; bomb tests that assert a refusal under GOMEMLIMIT, and the safe defaults of eval.Options; performance against the reference, single core, once a function is on a hot path.
data.how-it-is-measured#How it is measured: testdata/base/exports.tsv: the 1 362 functions exported by base, with their kind (primitive or closure), generated by the oracle (R 4.6.2) and regenerated when R is bumped. testdata/base/needs.tsv: for each closure, the names of the .Internal functions it calls; internals.tsv: per internal, the number of call sites and of closures. They hold names and counts only, obtained from the running oracle; nothing of base’s source is kept. Coverage is the fraction of base exports that the evaluator implements and for which a passing golden exercises the function (a name that appears as a call in testdata/eval, whose snippets all agree with R). It is printed by go run ./cmd/rparity basecov and recorded in the README at each tag. A function counted once is not uncounted when more cases are added. A refusal (eval.Unsupported) counts as not implemented. The metric is deliberately a floor: one passing snippet per function is the entry ticket; the differential fuzz modes and the base R test suite (run through the oracle’s own snippet generator, never copied) are what make a function trustworthy. basecov also prints, from needs.tsv, the greedy order of the missing internals that completes the most closures, and the count of closures that need none (a rewrite suffices): 701 of the 1 042 closures not yet implemented at the time the plan was written. Base’s calls to .Internal are spread flat, so their frequency ranks nothing.
data.order-of-the-slices#Order of the slices: Slice Contents 4 (v0.7.0) the rest of M2: 65 primitives, factor, match, unique, collation 5 (v0.8.0, done: 22.2 %) vectors: the base library starts. Our own R in eval/baselib/*.R (BSD, written from help pages and oracle behaviour: isTRUE, xor, Negate, setNames, set operations, append, head, tail, ifelse, nrow/ncol, lengths, rep_len, diff, outer) and Go natives (as.vector, order, rank, pmax, pmin, which.max, which.min, tabulate, row and column sums and means, t, diag, mean, stopifnot); 1 202 of 1 202 goldens, vector fuzz 18 000 of 18 000. The rest of the plan’s list (vector, rev, table, apply, sweep, rowsum) is not claimed here 6 (v0.9.0, v0.9.1, done: 23.3 %) strings and text: strrep, substr<-, strtoi, make.unique, basename, dirname, formatC, prettyNum, toString, sQuote/dQuote/shQuote, noquote, file.path; then format(big.mark =), formatC(format = "fg"), match.arg. Strings fuzz (part 2) 16 000 of 16 000 after the first run’s 255 differences were fixed; sprintf/format fuzz 10 000 of 10 000, no exclusions; 1 252 goldens 7 (v0.10.0, done: 24.4 %) conditions and the call stack: withRestarts, computeRestarts, findRestart, invokeRestart, tryInvokeRestart, sys.nframe/sys.calls/sys.frames/sys.frame/sys.on.exit, Recall, match.call, errorCondition, warningCondition, geterrmessage; 1 302 of 1 302 goldens. Four listed divergences, see Evaluator 8 environments and namespaces 9 dates and times 10 connections and files 11 linear algebra and numerics that base exports (depends on go-numerics) 12 the complex and raw types, expression vectors, formulas, S4 A slice is tagged when its goldens, fuzz, FuzzEval and bomb tests are green and basecov has moved. Slices 5 onwards are planned, not started.
data.the-clean-room-rule-for-base-functions#T: Specification: R’s documentation and the observed behaviour of the oracle. Never read, never copied: the files of src/library/base/R, src/main, src/nmath, tests/. A function is written from its help page and from experiments: snippets in testdata/eval/*.R, turned into goldens by the oracle, and the code is made to agree. Two homes for the code: Go natives (eval/*.go) for hot paths and loops over vectors, and our own R (eval/baselib/*.R, embedded) for glue closures. .Internal itself is not provided (it is refused): base closures are rewritten and do not go through it. The 401 internals base calls are a measure of work, not an API to reproduce.

data.getting-the-oracle#Getting the oracle:
The tests that need R skip when Rscript is not found. To run them, install the pinned release, which conda-forge publishes for macOS arm64 and Linux x86-64, and point RGO_RSCRIPT at it:
micromamba create -y -p ~/r-4.6.2 -c conda-forge --override-channels r-base=4.6.2 export RGO_RSCRIPT=~/r-4.6.2/bin/Rscript RGO_REQUIRE_ORACLE=1 go test ./... # a missing R is a failure, not a skip go run ./cmd/roracle regen # rewrite testdata/golden RGO_REQUIRE_ORACLE=1 turns the skips into failures (CI sets it).
data.layout#Layout: Path Role rds/ R serialization reader and writer internal/oracle/ the driver of the reference R, and the R side of the protocol (oracle.R) internal/gen/ golden-file generators and readers cmd/roracle/ the command that regenerates the goldens testdata/ inputs written for this repository, and golden/
data.what-exists#What exists: internal/oracle starts one Rscript --vanilla process (the pinned release; any other version is refused at the greeting) and talks to it over stdin/stdout. Requests are R’s own serialization format, written by the Go rds package; replies are R serializations, one hex line each, so no JSON package is needed on the R side. Operations: eval, deparse, parsedata (utils::getParseData), describe, reserialize. Output, warnings and the condition class and message are captured and returned; each request gets a fresh environment; a per-call timeout kills R; R_MAX_VSIZE bounds its vector heap. The test suite starts a fake R from its own test binary, so the protocol and every failure mode are tested without R. rds reads and writes R’s serialization format (XDR, versions 2 and 3, gzip or bzip2 compressed): vectors of every atomic type, lists, pairlists, calls, symbols, closures, environments (with sharing and cycles), namespace and package references, built-ins, external pointers, S4 objects and ALTREP objects (kept in serialized form; Altrep.Materialize expands the compact sequences, wrappers and deferred strings). A decoded value encodes back to the same bytes: attributes in order, the object and general-purpose bits, string encoding flags, NaN payloads (NA_real_ is a NaN). Byte-code and promises are refused. The decoder is built for untrusted input: size limit after decompression (decompression bombs are refused), nesting limit, every claimed length checked against the bytes left before allocating. It is fuzzed (FuzzDecode, corpus in rds/testdata/fuzz). Since go-embedded-r/r pull request 25 an ALTREP object found in a version-2 stream is expanded, as R’s reader does (its ReadItem has no version test, while WriteItem emits ALTREP only for version 3 or later), so the decoded tree is always writable by the version-2 encoder; an unknown ALTREP class is a decode error, and the expansion is bounded by a cumulative budget of MaxBytes/8 elements. Version 3 is unchanged. cmd/roracle regenerates the golden files (roracle regen), prints the identity of the R that answers (roracle version) and evaluates a snippet (roracle eval 'expr'). Goldens (testdata/golden): deparse.jsonl is parse + deparse of the snippets in testdata/snippets.R (the input of the M1 parser), and rds.jsonl is serialize() of the expressions of testdata/values.R. Both inputs are written for this repository. The tests replay the goldens without R: every value R serialized decodes, agrees with R’s typeof and length, and re-encodes to R’s exact bytes; values built in Go encode to the bytes R writes. With R, the live tests check that R reads Go’s bytes back unchanged and that regenerating the goldens reproduces the committed files.

data:
The package is github.com/go-embedded-r/r/syntax; the parser was released in v0.1.0 and deparse completes M1 in v0.2.0 (see Deparse).
f, err := syntax.ParseAll(src) // or ParseAllLimits(src, syntax.Limits{MaxBytes, MaxDepth, MaxNodes}) names, err := syntax.TopLevelNames(cell) // names a cell assigns and reads lines := syntax.Deparse(f.Exprs[0], nil) // deparse(), one string per line
data.bounds#Bounds: Bytes, tree depth (also for chains such as a+a+a+..., built by a loop) and node count; R’s own 50-level context stack (contextstack overflow). Bomb tests (200 000-deep chains of every shape) assert a refusal under a memory limit.
data.errors#Errors: *syntax.Error has Line, Col and Message, and its text is the message parse() signals, byte for byte, source context and caret included. Limits give a *syntax.LimitError (wraps ErrLimit). The statements before an error are kept in the returned File.
data.known-gaps#Known gaps: The effect of #line directives on the line numbers of later errors; parse(file=) encoding options; an invalid UTF-8 input is parsed as R’s lexer does, and for such text R cannot produce parse data, so tokens are not compared.
data.numbers#Numbers: A decimal literal is computed in double precision, digit by digit with an explicit fused multiply-add (math.FMA), then scaled by a power of ten: what R does on macOS arm64, where long double is double and the compiler fuses 10*ans + digit. 150 000 random literals are identical to that R’s, bit for bit, and the result is the same on every platform. R on x86-64 Linux accumulates in 80-bit extended precision and can differ by one unit in the last place on literals of more than 15 digits (the CI oracle lane saw it on 1e300), and by up to 6 ulp on literals near the subnormal range (measured on R’s own tests/: 290 literals differ, at most by 6 ulp). The parser is deterministic and matches the 64-bit reference; the platform-dependent literals are in testdata/numbers.R, compared within 16 ulp and kept out of the goldens. One literal differs by more: 1.7976931348623157e308 (the largest double) is Inf in 64-bit-double R and in the Go parser, and is kept by 80-bit R. Hexadecimal literals follow R’s rule (0x1.8p1).
data.parity-with-r-462#Parity with R 4.6.2:
Judged by the oracle, never by expectations written by hand: go run ./cmd/rparity ... parses the same text with R and with Go and compares
the terminal tokens and positions with getParseData(); the tree with a dump of the language objects of parse(keep.source = FALSE) (names, constants as IEEE bits, empty arguments, formals); the error text with parse()’s; the output of deparse() and print() (see Deparse). R’s own sources are read where they are unpacked and never committed.
Corpus Inputs Tree Tokens Deparse Error text, byte for byte R src/library: every .R file of the base packages (7.8 MB) 844 (842 parse, 2 rejected) 842 / 842 842 / 842 842 / 842 2 / 2 R tests/: 95 files (1 is not UTF-8 and is skipped) 94 (90 parse, 4 rejected) 90 / 90 90 / 90 90 / 90 4 / 4 our snippets (testdata/snippets.R) 42 42 / 42 42 / 42 42 / 42 n/a our error cases (testdata/errors.R) 52 (1 parses) 1 / 1 1 / 1 1 / 1 51 / 51 our edge cases: Unicode, raw strings, |>, \(x), ->>, hex/L/i numbers (testdata/edge.R) 88 (3 rejected) 85 / 85 85 / 85 85 / 85 3 / 3 our deparse cases: parentheses, precedence, line breaking, indentation, constants, names (testdata/deparse.R) 65 (2 rejected) 63 / 63 63 / 63 63 / 63 2 / 2 odd input: CRLF, tabs, form feeds, Unicode spaces, bidi controls, invalid UTF-8, =>, 50 and 5000 parentheses (parity.Extras, values.R) 120 all all all all differential fuzz: 610 000 random edits of lines of R’s sources (seeds 21, 31, 41, 42) 610 000 (about two thirds rejected) all all all all decimal literals, random (up to 20 digits, exponents -330..330) 100 000 100 000 identical doubles 99 995 identical, 5 not
data.speed#Speed: One core each, interleaved rounds, median of 11 after a warm-up round, 1-minute load 7.8 on an Apple M-series laptop: the 842 files of src/library that both parse (7.8 MB) take 0.214 s in Go (syntax.ParseAll, which also builds the source map and the token list) and 0.269 s in R’s parse(text =, keep.source = FALSE): Go/R = 0.80 (go run ./cmd/rparity bench DIR).
data.the-tree#The tree: R’s own shape: operators, if/for/{/[ and the rest are calls to a symbol; Function carries the formals; |> is rewritten as R does; -> is <- with the sides swapped; a string callee is a symbol. Every node has a Span (line, column and byte range). File.Tokens are the terminals of getParseData() (SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL, SYMBOL_SUB, EQ_FORMALS, COMMENT, LINE_DIRECTIVE…).
data.toplevelnames#TopLevelNames: Assigned: <-, =, ->, "x" <-, f(x) <-, x$a <- (assign x), assign("lit", ...), for variables. Read: free variables and called names not bound earlier in the cell, under R scoping (function parameters and locals, local(); a function body may use anything the cell assigns anywhere). Dynamic (with Reasons) when names cannot be resolved: <<-, assign/get with a computed name or another environment, eval, parse, source, attach, library, require, sys.function, environment<-, load, list2env…

Status: in development. M0, M1 and M2 are done, released as v0.7.0 of go-embedded-r/r; M3 started in v0.8.0 and the current release is v0.10.0 (slices 1 to 3 were v0.3.0 to v0.5.0, whose regex v0.6.0 replaced with a port of TRE; slice 2 was v0.3.0; v0.4.0 makes the Eval limits bounded by default, see Eval API; the parser was v0.1.0, deparse v0.2.0). The plan is bib/r.md of go-scikit/roadmap. Every stage is checked against the pinned GNU R 4.6.2, never against expectations written by hand.
Milestone Contents State M0 oracle harness internal/oracle, cmd/roracle, rds (serialization reader and writer), golden files done M1 parser syntax: lexer, parser, AST with source map, tokens, R’s parse errors, deparse, TopLevelNames done M2 evaluator eval: values, environments, promises, closures, control flow, replacement functions, subsetting, attributes, S3 dispatch, conditions, printing, the Eval API with limits; 175 of the 210 primitives (the other 35 refused with an explanatory error) and 110 base closures, environments as values, the apply family, character functions, regular expressions (a port of TRE, go-embedded-r/tre), the math group, factors, matching, collation done, slices 1 to 4 (v0.7.0); see Evaluator, Regular expressions and Eval API M3 base R the rest of what library(base) exports, rewritten clean room; 24.4 % of base’s 1 362 exports agree with R 4.6.2 at v0.10.0 (23.3 % at v0.9.0, 22.2 % at v0.8.0, 19.8 % at v0.7.0, 14.4 % at v0.6.0); slices 5 to 7 done (vectors, strings, conditions and the call stack) in progress; see M3 plan / base coverage M4 to M8 stats, graphics, notebook bridge, WebAssembly playground, CRAN ports planned Nothing in the M4 to M8 row exists yet. The README’s table groups M3 to M8 as “base, stats, regex, graphics, notebook bridge, wasm playground, CRAN ports”; the split of M4 onwards is not assigned subject by subject there, and this page does not assign it either.
data.known-gaps-of-m1#Known gaps of M1: the effect of #line directives on the line numbers of later errors; parse(file=) encoding options; an invalid UTF-8 input is parsed as R’s lexer does, and for such text R cannot produce parse data, so its tokens are not compared; numeric constants that deparse differently on some platforms: see Deparse. See The parser for the parity measurements.

data:
Since v0.6.0 (pull request 11, 2026-11-06), R’s regular expressions are TRE. The matcher is github.com/go-embedded-r/tre v0.1.0 (see The tre module), a Go port of TRE, the engine R uses for its default patterns (perl = FALSE, fixed = FALSE). It replaces the approximation on Go’s regexp of v0.5.0, whose lazy quantifiers, capture priority in repeated groups and \</\> differed from R.
grepl, grep, sub, gsub, regexpr, gregexpr, regmatches and strsplit use it. Lazy quantifiers, capture priority in repeated groups, back-references ((a)\\1, run by TRE’s backtracking matcher) and \< \> behave as in R. R’s choice of byte mode for all-ASCII input and wide mode otherwise is reproduced, with its quirks: an error text without the pattern for grepl and regexpr in wide mode, and the empty-match tokens of strsplit.
data.judged-by-r#Judged by R: Check Result R-level differential fuzz: random POSIX extended patterns, with lazy quantifiers, back-references, \< \> \b and non-ASCII text, through grepl, sub, gsub, regexpr, gregexpr, strsplit, regmatches (--mode regex; seeds 1, 7, 21; each function reported on its own line; nothing excluded) 60 000 / 60 000 goldens of testdata/eval, including regular expressions, against R 4.6.2 1 302 / 1 302 (v0.10.0) The port itself is also checked against upstream TRE; see The tre module.
data.memory-bounded-on-every-target#Memory: b: tre’s README has a “Limits and memory” section: the compile limits (MaxPattern 65 536, MaxNodes 2^17, MaxStates and MaxTransitions 2^19, MaxSetItems 2^17, MaxSteps 2^28) and a lazy DFA capped at 2 048 states. Measured peaks: every bomb test stays under 256 MiB on every target, wasm included, asserted by the tests; the whole bomb suite peaks at 124 MiB under wazero. Before tre v0.1.3 the deep-nesting pattern took 3.5 GiB. See The tre module.
data.related-limits-of-slice-3#Related limits: sort of non-atomic values is not implemented. sort and ls follow R’s ICU collation for Latin text since v0.7.0 (see M3 plan / base coverage).
data.rs-own-tre-behind-rcompat#R’s own TRE, b: R 4.6.2 ships a modified copy of TRE. The port’s Options.RCompat reproduces the behaviours where that copy differs from upstream ({,n}, bound overflow, the backtracking restart test, shared bracket positions, negated classes in copies of a repetition), so that go-embedded-r/r answers like R. They were found by diffing R’s copy against upstream, used as a specification only: no R source is copied, and the behaviours are judged by R itself.
data.speed-an-open-defect#Speed: an open defe:
grepl is 1.44 times slower than R 4.6.2 (Go time over R time), measured when tre v0.1.0 shipped: load 5.3, 5 interleaved rounds, one core, 20 000 lines. By the fleet rule, slower than the reference is an open defect: go-embedded-r/tre issue 3. The other cases of the same table: gsub with a class 0.87, gsub with a group 1.13 (also above 1), regexpr 0.92, back-references 0.99.
tre v0.1.1 (2026-11-07, pull request 7) adds a lazily built DFA for yes/no matches, used when no assertion depends on the position, and a start-position skip in the backtracker. Engine level, go test -bench, 20 000 lines, Apple M4: the grepl case [0-9]+@host[0-9]+\.example went from 5.95 ms to 0.69 ms; a back-reference case from 7.6 ms to 7.2 ms; the engines of regexpr and gsub with a group are unchanged. The end-to-end ratio against R has not been measured since: the machine’s load was far above the measuring limit of 8, so the tool refused. Issue 3 stays open until the table is measured at load 8 or below; the 1.44 above is the last measured figure.
go-embedded-r/r v0.7.1 also streams the loop of sub and gsub around the engine (matches are streamed, the replacement is parsed once, texts without a match ask the engine only for a yes/no, sub stops at its first match): BenchmarkGsubGroup, 20 000 lines, 247k to 87k allocations per operation and 9.0 to 4.6 MB per operation. Allocation counts are exact; no timing against R is claimed, because the load was above the measuring limit.
data.what-still-differs#What still differs: Approximate matching ({~1}, {+n}): the syntax is not ported and is an error. Non-ASCII classes follow Go’s Unicode tables, not a C library’s iswctype, so classes of non-ASCII characters can differ from R’s. perl = TRUE (PCRE) is refused: the call stops with an error that says it is not supported. Exponential backtracking is refused by a step limit, not run to the end. Some other pathological patterns are refused by limits too (pattern size, AST nodes, NFA states). useBytes and the multibyte-locale narrow API are not modelled. Patterns beyond the compile limits are refused (tre v0.1.3, in go-embedded-r/r v0.8.1): nesting thousands deep, huge repetition expansion, more than about 2^17 nodes. The call stops with regular expression '...' is too large for this evaluator (the engine’s ErrESpace). No golden or fuzz case reaches these limits, but R compiles some of those patterns, so some extreme patterns R accepts are now refused.

data:
github.com/go-embedded-r/tre (v0.1.0, 2026-11-06, pull request 1) is a pure-Go port of TRE, the POSIX regular expression engine (leftmost-longest, submatch addressing with tags, lazy quantifiers, back-references, \< \> \b \w \d \s, (?i) and friends) that R uses for its default patterns. It is what go-embedded-r/r runs since v0.6.0.
re, err := tre.Compile(`(a|ab)(c|bcd)(d*)`, tre.Extended) m, err := re.ExecString("abcd", 4, 0) // []tre.Match{{0,4},{0,1},{1,4},{4,4}} Offsets are in characters (UTF-8 decoded), or bytes with tre.UseBytes.
data.how-it-is-checked#How it is checked: TRE’s own tests: upstream’s tests/retest.c is run through a recording wrapper and replayed against the port: 286 compilations and 3514 executions (wide) and 3510 (narrow) with byte-for-byte equal return codes and match offsets. Excluded and counted: the 4 narrow-API patterns of retest’s EUC-JP section (20 executions), which run in a multibyte locale the port does not have. Differential fuzz against upstream TRE built as C: 197,588 compared, 0 mismatches. Excluded and counted: 2,410 approximate-matching patterns, 1 backtracking case cut by the step limit. R 4.6.2 for the R-level behaviour, through the regex fuzz of go-embedded-r/r (60 000 / 60 000, see Regular expressions). A fuzz target, bomb tests that assert refusals under GOMEMLIMIT and ulimit -v, govulncheck, 3 OSes with -race, 386, every GOOS, wasm.
data.licence#Licence: BSD 2-Clause, with the TRE notice kept in the repository’s NOTICE file. It is ported from upstream TRE at commit 71bfcaf (lib/tre-parse.c, tre-compile.c, tre-match-parallel.c, tre-match-backtrack.c, regexec.c): parse, AST, tagged NFA, the parallel matcher, and the backtracking matcher used only when the pattern has back-references.
data.limits-and-memory#Limits and memory:
A hostile pattern or subject gets an error (ErrESpace, ErrSteps), never an out-of-memory or a hang. The limits (pull request 10 documents them in the README):
Limit Default Bounds MaxPattern 65 536 pattern length in code units MaxNodes 2^17 AST nodes, including bounded-repetition copies MaxStates 2^19 NFA positions MaxTransitions 2^19 NFA transitions MaxSetItems 2^17 firstpos/lastpos entries, and the parent lists of nested groups MaxSteps 2^28 work of one match (ErrSteps); mainly for back-references The lazy DFA that answers yes/no matches is capped too: at most 2 048 DFA states and 2^18 NFA-state entries over all of them (about 2 MiB). At either cap it is switched off for that regexp and the NFA matcher answers, with the same result.
A pattern over a limit is refused with ErrESpace. This includes some patterns that R accepts: very deep group nesting (thousands of levels) and very large repetition expansions such as ((a{255}){255}){255}.
Memory guarantee. Measured peaks (the Go runtime’s Sys high-water mark over the bomb tests; nested counts, quadratic sets, 30 000 nested groups, a 2^20-state DFA, exponential back-reference backtracking): every bomb stays under 256 MiB on every target, wasm included, asserted by the tests (peak_test.go). The whole bomb suite peaks at 124 MiB under wazero, and the DFA bomb alone at 17 MiB natively. Before v0.1.3 the deep-nesting pattern took 3.5 GiB.
data.not-ported-and-open-issues#Not ported, a: Approximate matching ({~n}, {+n}, {1i+1d<2}): a pattern using it fails with ErrApprox. The C library’s system-wctype, multibyte-string and user-string front ends: one engine over []rune code units replaces them. Character classes use Go’s unicode tables, so classes of non-ASCII characters can differ from a given C library’s iswctype. Open: issue 3, grepl is 1.44 times slower than R 4.6.2; issue 4, upstream TRE reads one byte past the pattern in tre_regncompb.
data.rcompat#RCompat:
Options.RCompat reproduces the behaviours of R 4.6.2’s modified copy of TRE where they differ from upstream, so that go-embedded-r/r answers like R:
{,n} keeps a minimum of -1, so it matches n+1 repetitions (^a{,3}$ matches aaaa); a bound that overflows an int means “unbounded, or 1”; a bound above 255 is “Invalid contents of {}”; {m,n} expands to (|x(|x)) rather than (x(x)?)?. An empty REG_LITERAL pattern matches the empty string. The backtracking matcher decides whether to retry from a later start position by the current character instead of the character at the start of the attempt: ([abc]+)\w*\1 does not match banana in R. The items of a bracket expression (and the two cases of an (?i) literal) share one NFA position. tre_copy_ast forgets the negated classes of a copied literal: in wide mode [^[:space:]]{1,3} matches a space on its repetitions. Messages and limits: no TRE_MAX_RE, no REG_BADMAX, assert becomes an R error, one extra text for tre_version. R’s changes are GPL and were used as specification only; the behaviours are re-implemented and judged by R itself.
data.v011#v0.1.1: v0.1.1 (2026-11-07, pull request 7) adds a lazily built DFA for yes/no matches (used when no assertion depends on the position) and a start-position skip in the backtracker. Engine-level grepl case: 5.95 ms to 0.69 ms on 20 000 lines. The speed ratio against R is not yet measured (load too high); issue 3 stays open.
data.v012-and-v013#v0.1.2 and v0.1.3: Both 2026-11-07. v0.1.2 (pull request 8) bounds the lazy DFA and adds a bomb test. v0.1.3 (pull request 9) bounds the compile memory for the wasm32 heap: tighter default limits, a parent-list budget, and a peak-memory assertion in every bomb test, with no wasm skip. Some extreme patterns that R accepts are now refused (ErrESpace; through go-embedded-r/r v0.8.1 the message is regular expression '...' is too large for this evaluator); see Regular expressions.
